prompt.context: Your client is Heavy Things Fitness, a small fitness center chain with 15 locations in a minor metropolitan area in the US, established during the fitness boom in the late 70s. After decades of continual growth, Heavy Things has seen membership decline by alarming rates. Over the past 5 years, it has seen total membership numbers decrease an average of 6% annually.
prompt.question: The client has asked us to determine what is causing this trend and how they can reverse this trend to begin growing again. Based on what you know about this industry, what do you believe is causing this membership attrition?

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of the city?
clarifying_info.a: The city has a population of about 1-1.5M, similar to Providence, RI; Milwaukee, WI; or Jacksonville, FL.

clarifying_info.q: What services does Heavy Things Fitness offer?
clarifying_info.a: Heavy Things Fitness gyms offer cardio rooms, free weights, and weight machines.

clarifying_info.q: How do Heavy Things prices compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Membership prices and payment plans are in line with their closest competitors.
Heavy Things Fitness targets serious fitness enthusiasts, believing that these are the most loyal customers.

clarifying_info.q: How are overall gym memberships in this city trending?
clarifying_info.a: Gym memberships in this city have been growing 3% each year, both in this city and in all regions of the country.

framework: Diagnose root cause of 6% annual membership decline despite overall market growing 3% annually
Analyze market-level trends: shifting demographics, changing fitness preferences, competitive dynamics
Analyze client-specific factors: service offerings, pricing, customer profile, facility quality
Compare client demographic mix vs. market demographic trends to identify mismatch
Identify target segment(s) with growth potential
Develop strategic options to reach new target segments while managing cannibalization risk
Evaluate conversion vs. expansion financially to determine most profitable path
Deliver recommendation with risks and next steps

questions.prompt: What do you believe is causing Heavy Things' membership decline?
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify that the market overall is growing (3% annually) while Heavy Things declines 6%, implying Heavy Things is losing share. Potential causes include: changing fitness trends toward class-based or high-intensity training; negative client attributes such as poor customer service or deteriorating facilities; competitors offering superior services (personal trainers, basketball courts); demographic shifts away from Heavy Things' target demographic. Candidates should rule out declining city population (rest of market is growing) and price differences (already comparable to competitors).

questions.prompt: Given the information in Exhibits 1 and 2, what do you believe is the source of Heavy Things' declining membership?
questions.guidance: Exhibit 1 shows that local gym memberships are trending toward Gen X (40-50) and Gen Y (30-40) and away from Millennials, Baby Boomers, and Seniors. Exhibit 2 shows Heavy Things' membership is heavily concentrated in Millennials (62%), precisely the declining segment. Key takeaway: Heavy Things' demographic profile is misaligned with market growth — it is over-indexed on the declining Millennial segment and under-indexed on the growing Gen X and Y segments. Potential conclusions: target Gen X and Y customers, or become a niche gym for the declining Millennial segment.

questions.prompt: What are some possible ways Heavy Things Fitness can target Gen X and Y customers? What would be the risks of each solution?
questions.guidance: Good solutions include: (1) Marketing campaign targeting consumers aged 30-50 with appropriate spokesperson, ad placement in areas of interest, and messaging that positions the gym for these consumers. (2) Offer new services more appealing to middle-aged customers. (3) Adjust pricing — if price is a concern, lower prices; if not, raising prices could fund more services and deter younger members with less disposable income. (4) Make the gym an exclusive club. Top candidates must address cannibalization risk: switching target demographic risks losing existing Millennial members. Mitigation strategies include: convert only some locations while keeping others unchanged so current members can transfer; develop a brand extension in new clubs; divide physical space of each gym into two distinct gym identities.

questions.prompt: Is it more profitable to convert 5 existing Heavy Things locations to Fast Class Fitness, or to open 5 new Fast Class properties?
questions.guidance: Candidate should first identify what information is needed (revenues and costs for both scenarios). The key insight is that Fast Class revenues and costs are identical under both options, so the only difference is the cost of maintaining 5 additional Heavy Things locations vs. the lost revenue from closing them. Convert scenario yields $35K/month profit; Expand scenario yields $5K/month profit. Converting is more profitable.

math.setup: Compare monthly profit under two scenarios: (A) Convert 5 Heavy Things to Fast Class; (B) Expand by opening 5 new Fast Class locations while keeping all 15 Heavy Things open. Fast Class revenues and costs are identical in both scenarios. The difference is whether 10 or 15 Heavy Things locations operate, with conversion capturing 33% member retention.
steps: CONVERT SCENARIO — Costs (monthly): Heavy Things Rent: 10 locations x $10K = $100K; Heavy Things Labor: 10 locations x 2 employees x $3K = $60K; Fast Class Rent: 5 locations x $10K = $50K; Fast Class Labor: 5 locations x 4 employees x $4K = $80K; Total Costs = $290K

CONVERT SCENARIO — Revenues (monthly): Heavy Things current members: 10 locations x 300 members x $50 = $150K; Heavy Things retained members (from converted gyms): 5 locations x 33% x 300 members x $50 = $25K; Fast Class: 5 locations x 400 members x $75 = $150K; Total Revenues = $325K

EXPAND SCENARIO — Costs (monthly): Heavy Things Rent: 15 locations x $10K = $150K; Heavy Things Labor: 15 locations x 2 employees x $3K = $90K; Fast Class Rent: 5 locations x $10K = $50K; Fast Class Labor: 5 locations x 4 employees x $4K = $80K; Total Costs = $370K
EXPAND SCENARIO — Revenues (monthly): Heavy Things: 15 locations x 300 members x $50 = $225K; Fast Class: 5 locations x 400 members x $75 = $150K; Total Revenues = $375K

CONCLUSION: Convert ($35K/month) is more profitable than Expand ($5K/month). Shortcut: Fast Class is constant across both, so compare only the difference — maintaining 5 extra Heavy Things costs $80K/month extra but retains only $50K in revenue, a net loss of $30K vs. converting.
math.answer: Convert scenario yields $35K/month profit vs. $5K/month for expand scenario. Conversion is more profitable by $30K/month.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some possible ways that Heavy Things Fitness can target Gen X and Y customers?

categories.name: Marketing
ideas: Run a targeted marketing campaign for consumers aged 30-50
Use a spokesperson in the 30-50 age range
Place ads in media channels frequented by Gen X and Y
Develop messaging that explicitly positions the gym as designed for these consumers (similar to Planet Fitness approach)

categories.name: Service Offerings
ideas: Introduce class-based fitness programs popular with middle-aged customers
Add amenities appealing to Gen X and Y such as basketball courts or group fitness studios

categories.name: Pricing Strategy
ideas: Lower prices if price is a primary barrier for target demographic
Raise prices to fund premium services and to naturally filter out younger, lower-income members

categories.name: Brand and Positioning
ideas: Create an exclusive membership club limited to 30-50 age group
Develop a brand extension (e.g., Fast Class Fitness) targeting Gen X and Y
Convert select locations to Gen X/Y-focused establishments while keeping others unchanged

categories.name: Cannibalization Mitigation
ideas: Convert only some locations to maintain options for existing Millennial members
Keep remaining Heavy Things locations so converted-gym members can transfer
Divide physical gym space into two distinct branded areas
Launch Fast Class as a fully separate brand in new locations

recommendation: Convert five Heavy Things Fitness centers to Fast Class Fitness centers, a brand extension focused on class-based fitness programs that appeal to Gen X and Y customers
This conversion strategy generates $35K/month in profit vs. $5K/month under expansion, making it significantly more financially attractive
risks: Five may not be the optimal number of locations to convert — further analysis could identify the profit-maximizing conversion count
The 33% member retention estimate may be inaccurate — actual retention could be higher or lower, affecting financial projections
Expanding to new properties (Expand scenario) would serve as additional advertising and brand presence, potentially generating memberships not captured in the model
Risk of brand confusion if Fast Class is not clearly differentiated from Heavy Things
Remaining Millennial members at Heavy Things locations may continue to decline without a separate strategy for that segment
next_steps: Hire class instructors and personal trainers for the five new Fast Class locations
Develop an advertising and brand-building campaign for the Fast Class brand targeting Gen X and Y consumers
Hire contractors to physically convert Heavy Things gym spaces into Fast Class fitness centers
Monitor membership retention rates at remaining Heavy Things locations and adjust conversion count if needed
Evaluate whether additional Heavy Things locations should be converted based on profitability analysis
